passage: I'm Ishita, and last Thursday I opened a message from Mahima that was eleven lines long. It started with the client meeting, wandered through the office move and ended with "so thoughts?" Thoughts on what? I read it three times on the bus. I told myself I would reply later, and by nine at night I still hadn't, because I couldn't tell whether she needed a decision, a file or just sympathy. Next morning I guessed she wanted the March figures and sent a spreadsheet. It turned out she wanted a date for the review. We lost half a day. Honestly, I felt uneasy and a bit annoyed, because the work of figuring it out landed on me.

qa.q: How many lines long was Mahima's message?
qa.a: It was eleven lines long.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling as the message was read three times on the bus?
qa.a: Confused and uneasy, unable to tell what was needed.

qa.q: What could Ishita have done before guessing?
qa.a: Ask Mahima one short question, such as whether a decision, a file or a date was needed.

qa.q: What might have been in Mahima's mind when ending with "so thoughts?"
qa.a: Mahima likely assumed Ishita already knew what was being asked, so the question felt clear to the writer while it left Ishita guessing.

grounding: Shows a busy colleague who cannot tell what a rambling message wants, delays, guesses wrongly and carries the interpretation work.

passage: I'm Vidya, and I sit across from Vijay in the finance team. Yesterday around noon Vijay read a message from operations, frowned, scrolled up and down, and read it again. It was one long paragraph about a delayed invoice, a vendor's email and "the usual thing", with no question in it. Vijay muttered, "Do they want me to pay or to wait?" Twice Vijay picked up the phone and put it down. Finally Vijay replied, "Sorry, do you need a payment released today?" An answer came an hour later: no, just information. By then the lunch break and another task had slipped. I don't know how long Vijay had been stuck before I noticed.

qa.q: What did Vijay mutter after reading the message?
qa.a: Vijay muttered, "Do they want me to pay or to wait?"

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when the phone was picked up and put down twice?
qa.a: Uncertain and hesitant, unsure whether asking would look silly, since the message had no question in it.

qa.q: What useful step did Vijay take at the end?
qa.a: Vijay asked one direct question about whether a payment was needed today.

qa.q: What can and can't Vidya know about Vijay's state from watching?
qa.a: Vidya can see the frowning, muttering and phone handling, but cannot be sure how long Vijay was stuck or exactly what worried Vijay.

grounding: Shows a colleague watching another read a rambling message, unable to tell what is needed and losing time.

passage:
Eshaan was on the 7:40 local, squeezed against the door, when Kavitha's message arrived. The network kept dropping, so it loaded in pieces.
"Hi! So about Thursday, the client said maybe the meeting moves, or maybe not, they were unsure about the room, also Pradeep might join, and the deck needs a few changes, not sure which, and they mentioned the budget sheet? Anyway let me know!!"
Eshaan read it three times between stations. Let her know what? Was he supposed to attend? Change the deck? Send the budget? He had four other messages waiting and a standup at nine.
He guessed. At the office he spent an hour updating the budget sheet and emailed it to the client.
At noon Kavitha called. "Why did you send them the budget? I only needed you to check if you were free on Thursday."
Eshaan put the phone down and rubbed his eyes. An hour gone, and an awkward email to take back.

qa.q: On which train was Eshaan when the message arrived?
qa.a: He was on the 7:40 local.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel after Kavitha's call at noon?
qa.a: Eshaan felt frustrated and tired, rubbing his eyes over an hour lost to the wrong guess.

qa.q: What could Kavitha have written instead?
qa.a: Kavitha could have asked one clear question first, such as whether Eshaan was free on Thursday, and left the maybes out.

qa.q: If you were Kavitha, what would you want to change after this call?
qa.a: Kavitha would probably want to write shorter messages with the exact request, since the rambling one cost them both time.

grounding: Shows a busy colleague who cannot tell what a rambling message needs, guesses wrongly and loses time.

passage:
In the accounts office in Koramangala, Anjali's inbox had forty-three unread emails. Himani's was the longest.
It began with how the audit had gone last year, moved on to a vendor who was always late, mentioned a spreadsheet "somewhere on the shared drive," and ended with three questions tangled in one paragraph. Anjali scrolled down, scrolled up, and still could not tell whether Himani wanted numbers, a meeting or just to vent.
She flagged it. Later, she told herself. Later became two days.
On Thursday Himani messaged, "Did you see my email? It's urgent." Anjali felt a flash of irritation, then guilt. She opened the email again, took a pen and wrote on a sticky note: "Question 1? Question 2? Deadline?" It took her twenty minutes to pull the three questions apart.
She replied with three numbered answers and one line at the end: "Next time, could you put the questions at the top?"

qa.q: How many unread emails did Anjali have?
qa.a: Anjali's inbox had forty-three unread emails.

qa.q: What did Anjali feel when Himani messaged that it was urgent?
qa.a: Anjali felt a flash of irritation, then guilt, because she had delayed the unclear email for two days.

qa.q: What small request at the end could help both of them next time?
qa.a: Asking Himani to put the questions at the top, so the reader does not have to dig them out.

qa.q: How might the delay have looked from Himani's side?
qa.a: Himani was probably worried and impatient, not knowing that her long email was the reason no reply came.

grounding: Illustrates a busy colleague who cannot tell what a rambling email needs, delays replying and has to do the work of interpreting it.

passage:
"Dilnaz, got a minute?" Raghav held up his phone at her desk.
"Sure. What's up?"
"Your message last night. 'Please sort the thing for Friday, the usual but more, and not like last time.' What thing?"
Dilnaz laughed. "The snacks! For the client visit."
"I thought you meant the printouts. I printed fifty copies of the report this morning."
"Fifty? Raghav, they're bringing laptops."
"How was I supposed to know? 'The usual but more' could be anything."
Dilnaz winced. "Sorry. I wrote it in the cab, half asleep."
"And 'not like last time'?"
"Last time the samosas were cold."
Raghav put the phone down and sighed. "So I've wasted a ream of paper and I still have to order snacks."
"Let me write it properly." She typed: "Friday 11 a.m. client visit: order hot snacks for 12 people by Thursday 5 p.m." "Better?"
"Much. Next time, just that."

qa.q: How many copies of the report did Raghav print?
qa.a: Raghav printed fifty copies of the report.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel when he found out the message meant snacks?
qa.a: Raghav felt frustrated and a little annoyed, having wasted a ream of paper on the wrong guess.

qa.q: What made Dilnaz's second message clearer?
qa.a: It gave the time, the event, what to order, for how many people and by when, all in one line.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz see her first message once Raghav explains?
qa.a: Dilnaz is embarrassed and apologetic, admitting she wrote it in the cab, half asleep.

grounding: Shows a colleague who guesses wrongly from a vague message and has to redo work, because unclear writing left him to interpret it.

passage: Looking back, the message wasn't even long, but it ate my whole Tuesday. I'm Keerthana, and I coordinate transport for our school. Imran, who was organising annual day, sent this at 7 a.m.: "Hi, so annual day, you know how last year the buses were late and parents were upset, and this year the venue is the new auditorium which is further, and I was thinking about timing, maybe 5, maybe 5:30, principal hasn't confirmed, anyway the parents, can you see about it? Thanks!!" See about what? Buses? Parking? A notice? I read it four times on the staffroom sofa. I didn't want to look slow by asking. By lunch I guessed buses and booked three. At four, Imran called, puzzled. He'd only wanted to know how many parents needed a lift. Cancelling took an hour and an awkward call. The confusion was in his message, but the extra work had landed on me.

qa.q: How many buses did Keerthana book?
qa.a: Three.

qa.q: How did Keerthana feel reading the message on the staffroom sofa?
qa.a: Keerthana was confused and a bit anxious, reading it four times and not wanting to look slow by asking.

qa.q: What could Imran have written to save Keerthana's Tuesday?
qa.a: One clear line first, such as "Can you find out how many parents need a lift to the new auditorium, by Friday?", before any background.

qa.q: How did Imran see the situation when he called at four?
qa.a: Imran was puzzled by the buses, since the message seemed clear to him; he didn't realise the real question was buried in the ramble.

grounding: Shows a busy colleague who cannot tell what a rambling message wants, guesses wrongly, and ends up doing the work the unclear writing created.
